questions.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
questions.stem:
Three dry soil samples, X, Y and Z, were provided. Sample X feels gritty and does not form a ball when moistened; sample Y feels smooth and slightly sticky and forms a ball that crumbles; sample Z feels very sticky when wet and can be rolled into a thin thread.
To compare the air spaces in the soils, 50 cm3 of each dry soil was poured into a 100 cm3 measuring cylinder containing exactly 50 cm3 of water, stirred and allowed to stand until no more bubbles came out. The final volumes were: X - 82 cm3; Y - 78 cm3; Z - 75 cm3.
(a) Identify soil samples X, Y and Z by name. [3 marks]
(b) Explain why the bubbles came out of the soil. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate for each soil (i) the volume of air displaced; (ii) the percentage of air space by volume of soil. [6 marks]
(d) State two precautions to be taken in this experiment. [2 marks]
(e) State two importance of soil air to crops. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) X - sandy soil; Y - loamy soil; Z - clay soil (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) Water entered the pore spaces of the soil and displaced the air in them
6 marks: (c)(i) X: 100 - 82 = 18 cm3; Y: 22 cm3; Z: 25 cm3 (1 mark each); (ii) X: 18/50 x 100 = 36%; Y: 22/50 x 100 = 44%; Z: 25/50 x 100 = 50% (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d) Any two: soil must be completely dry; read the meniscus at eye level; stir to release all trapped air; use equal volumes of soil (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e) Any two: supplies oxygen for root respiration; oxygen for soil micro-organisms; aids decomposition of organic matter; aids germination (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) X is sandy soil, Y loamy soil and Z clay soil. (b) Water filled the pores and pushed out the air. (c) Without air, 50 cm3 soil + 50 cm3 water would give 100 cm3; the shortfall is the air: X 100 - 82 = 18 cm3 (18/50 x 100 = 36%); Y 22 cm3 (44%); Z 25 cm3 (50%). (d) Use dry soil, stir well, and read at eye level. (e) Soil air supplies oxygen for root and microbial respiration and aids germination.

questions.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
questions.stem:
Three glass tubes, each 30 cm long and plugged with cotton wool at the lower end, were filled with dry sandy soil, loamy soil and clay soil respectively, and stood together in a trough of water at the same depth. The height of water rise in each tube was recorded.
Time (min): 10, 20, 30, 60
Sandy soil (cm): 4.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5
Loamy soil (cm): 2.5, 4.5, 6.0, 8.5
Clay soil (cm): 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.5
(a) Name the soil property being investigated. [1 mark]
(b) Which soil showed (i) the fastest rate of rise in the first 10 minutes; (ii) the greatest height at 60 minutes? [2 marks]
(c) Calculate (i) the rate of rise in sandy soil during the first 10 minutes in cm/min; (ii) the average rate of rise in loamy soil over the 60 minutes, to two decimal places. [4 marks]
(d) Explain why water rose quickly at first in sandy soil but soon stopped rising. [3 marks]
(e) State two precautions taken in this experiment. [2 marks]
(f) State three importance of this property to crop production. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Capillarity (capillary rise of water)
2 marks: (b)(i) Sandy soil; (ii) loamy soil (1 mark each)
4 marks: (c)(i) 4.0 / 10 = 0.40 cm/min (2); (ii) 8.5 / 60 = 0.14 cm/min (2)
3 marks: (d) Sand has large pore spaces, so water moves through them quickly at first (1.5); but large pores have weak capillary pull, so water cannot be held up to a great height (1.5)
2 marks: (e) Any two: soils must be dry and equally packed; tubes of the same diameter; tubes stood at the same depth of water; readings taken at the same times (1 mark each)
3 marks: (f) Any three: brings water from lower layers to plant roots in dry season; brings dissolved nutrients up to the root zone; can bring salts to the surface (salinity) so it guides irrigation; helps seed germination (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) Capillarity. (b) Sand rose fastest in the first 10 minutes; loam reached the greatest height (8.5 cm) by 60 minutes. (c) Sand: 4.0 cm/10 min = 0.40 cm/min; loam: 8.5 cm/60 min = 0.14 cm/min (0.142). (d) Sand's large pores let water move quickly but exert weak capillary pull, so the column stops early; finer soils rise slowly but higher. (e) Use dry, evenly packed soils in identical tubes at the same depth. (f) Capillarity supplies water and nutrients to roots from below, aids germination and can bring salts up in dry areas.

questions.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
questions.stem:
Three funnels were each plugged with cotton wool and 100 g of oven-dried soil was placed in each: funnel A sandy soil, funnel B loamy soil, funnel C clay soil. Each funnel was placed over a measuring cylinder and 100 cm3 of water was poured slowly onto the soil. After one hour the volumes of water collected were: A - 70 cm3; B - 52 cm3; C - 38 cm3.
(a) What property of soil is being determined? [1 mark]
(b) Calculate the volume of water retained by each soil. [3 marks]
(c) Taking 1 cm3 of water as 1 g, calculate the water-holding capacity of each soil as a percentage of the dry mass of soil. [3 marks]
(d) Which soil (i) drains best; (ii) is most likely to become waterlogged? [2 marks]
(e) Why was the soil oven-dried before the experiment? [2 marks]
(f) Suggest two ways of improving the water-holding capacity of soil A. [2 marks]
(g) Why was the water poured slowly? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: (a) Water-holding (retention) capacity
3 marks: (b) A 30 cm3; B 48 cm3; C 62 cm3 (1 mark each)
3 marks: (c) A 30/100 x 100 = 30%; B 48%; C 62% (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d)(i) A (sandy); (ii) C (clay) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e) To remove all moisture so that the water retained is due only to the water added
2 marks: (f) Any two: add organic manure/compost; mulching; add clay/loam; cover cropping (1 mark each)
2 marks: (g) To allow the water to soak into the soil evenly and not overflow the funnel
questions.explanation: (a) Water-holding capacity. (b) Retained = 100 - collected: A 30 cm3, B 48 cm3, C 62 cm3. (c) With 1 cm3 = 1 g: A 30/100 x 100 = 30%, B 48%, C 62%. (d) Sandy soil drains best; clay is most likely to waterlog. (e) Oven-drying removes existing moisture. (f) Adding organic manure and mulching improve water retention of sandy soil. (g) Slow pouring lets water soak in evenly without overflowing.

questions.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on chemical properties of soil
questions.stem:
A student carried out the following tests on a soil sample from a school farm.
Test 1: an empty crucible weighed 20.00 g. Oven-dried soil was added and the crucible and soil weighed 45.00 g. After strong heating to constant mass and cooling in a desiccator, the crucible and soil weighed 43.50 g.
Test 2: a little soil was shaken with distilled water and filtered; a drop of universal indicator added to the filtrate gave an orange colour, which matched pH 5 on the colour chart.
Test 3: a little soil was placed in a test tube and dilute hydrochloric acid added; there was no effervescence.
(a) Calculate (i) the mass of dry soil used; (ii) the loss in mass on heating; (iii) the percentage organic matter in the soil. [5 marks]
(b) Is the soil acidic, neutral or alkaline? [1 mark]
(c) What does the result of Test 3 show? [2 marks]
(d) Name one material a farmer could apply to correct the soil reaction and state how it works. [3 marks]
(e) Name two crops that tolerate this soil reaction. [2 marks]
(f) Name an instrument for measuring soil pH directly in the field. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a)(i) 45.00 - 20.00 = 25.00 g (1); (ii) 45.00 - 43.50 = 1.50 g (1); (iii) 1.50/25.00 x 100 = 6.0% (3)
1 mark: (b) Acidic
2 marks: (c) The soil contains no (or very little) carbonates/lime (calcium carbonate)
3 marks: (d) Lime (agricultural lime/calcium carbonate, dolomite or wood ash) (1); it neutralises soil acidity, raising pH (2)
2 marks: (e) Any two: cassava, pineapple, tea, rice, Irish potato, cashew, oil palm (1 mark each)
2 marks: (f) Soil pH meter (or soil testing kit)
questions.explanation: (a) Dry soil = 45.00 - 20.00 = 25.00 g; loss on heating = 45.00 - 43.50 = 1.50 g; organic matter = 1.50/25.00 x 100 = 6.0%. (b) pH 5 is acidic. (c) No effervescence shows the soil has no carbonates. (d) Liming with agricultural lime or wood ash neutralises the acidity. (e) Cassava and pineapple tolerate acid soils. (f) A soil pH meter measures pH in the field.

questions.topic: Practical: Rocks
questions.stem:
Five rock specimens are described below.
Specimen P: hard, coarse-grained, speckled rock with interlocking crystals of glassy quartz, pink or white feldspar and black mica.
Specimen Q: whitish-grey rock which fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid and contains fossil shells.
Specimen R: white, crystalline, hard rock which fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid and has no fossils or layers.
Specimen S: rock made of rounded, sand-sized grains cemented together, rough to the touch, in layers.
Specimen T: fine-grained, soft rock that splits easily into thin layers and smells earthy when breathed on.
(a) Identify specimens P, Q, R, S and T. [5 marks]
(b) Classify each of P, Q and R as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic. [3 marks]
(c) From which rock is R formed and by what process? [2 marks]
(d) Name the gas given off when Q reacts with acid. [1 mark]
(e) Name the type of soil formed from the weathering of (i) S; (ii) T. [2 marks]
(f) State two uses of rock P. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) P - granite; Q - limestone; R - marble; S - sandstone; T - shale (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b) P - igneous; Q - sedimentary; R - metamorphic (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Limestone (1); metamorphism by heat and pressure (1)
1 mark: (d) Carbon dioxide
2 marks: (e)(i) Sandy soil; (ii) clay soil (1 mark each)
2 marks: (f) Any two: building/construction (chippings, gravel); road construction; monuments/tiles; source of soil minerals (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) P granite, Q limestone, R marble, S sandstone, T shale. (b) Granite is igneous, limestone sedimentary and marble metamorphic. (c) Marble forms from limestone by heat and pressure (metamorphism). (d) Calcium carbonate reacts with acid releasing carbon dioxide. (e) Sandstone weathers to sandy soil; shale to clay soil. (f) Granite is used for building and road construction.

questions.topic: Practical: Soil profile
questions.stem:
A soil pit dug on a farm near Ilorin showed the following layers from the surface downward.
Layer 1: 0-5 cm - dark brown, loose, with fresh and partly decayed leaves.
Layer 2: 5-30 cm - dark greyish-brown topsoil, crumbly, full of roots and earthworms.
Layer 3: 30-90 cm - reddish-brown, compact subsoil with few roots and some iron concretions.
Layer 4: 90-150 cm - partly weathered rock fragments mixed with soil.
Layer 5: below 150 cm - hard, unweathered rock.
(a) Name the horizon represented by each of layers 1 to 5. [5 marks]
(b) Calculate the thickness of each of layers 1 to 4. [2 marks]
(c) What percentage of the top 150 cm is layer 2? Give the answer to one decimal place. [2 marks]
(d) Explain why layer 2 is dark in colour and has many roots. [2 marks]
(e) Explain why layer 3 is reddish-brown and compact. [2 marks]
(f) State two uses of soil profile study to a farmer. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) 1 - O horizon (organic/litter layer); 2 - A horizon (topsoil); 3 - B horizon (subsoil); 4 - C horizon (weathered parent material); 5 - R/D horizon (bedrock) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) 5 cm, 25 cm, 60 cm, 60 cm (all four correct 2 marks; two or three correct 1 mark)
2 marks: (c) 25/150 x 100 = 16.7%
2 marks: (d) Rich in humus from decayed organic matter (1); loose, aerated and fertile so roots grow there (1)
2 marks: (e) Accumulation of iron oxides leached from above gives red colour (1); clay leached from above and lack of organic matter make it compact (1)
2 marks: (f) Any two: choice of crops with suitable rooting depth; decide on tillage/drainage; assess fertility and depth of soil; site selection for buildings/ponds (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) Layer 1 is the O horizon, 2 the A horizon (topsoil), 3 the B horizon (subsoil), 4 the C horizon and 5 bedrock (R). (b) Thicknesses: 5, 25, 60 and 60 cm. (c) 25/150 x 100 = 16.7%. (d) The topsoil is dark because of humus and holds many roots because it is loose and fertile. (e) The subsoil accumulates iron oxides and clay washed down (illuviation), making it red and compact. (f) Profile study guides choice of crops, tillage and drainage.

questions.topic: Practical: Farm tools and equipment
questions.stem:
Study the farm tools described below.
Tool A: a long, flat steel blade, about 50 cm long, sharpened along one edge, with a wooden handle.
Tool B: a flat, broad steel blade fixed at about a right angle to a short wooden handle; used in a swinging motion.
Tool C: a curved, sickle-shaped steel blade with a serrated or sharp inner edge and a short handle.
Tool D: a steel bar with a row of short teeth fixed at right angles to the end of a long handle.
Tool E: a steel blade, broad and scooped, with a long handle and a foot rest at the top of the blade.
(a) Identify tools A to E. [5 marks]
(b) State one use of each of tools A to E. [5 marks]
(c) State three maintenance practices for tool A. [3 marks]
(d) State two safety precautions to observe when using tool A. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - cutlass (machete); B - hoe; C - sickle; D - rake; E - spade (or shovel) (1 mark each)
5 marks: (b) A - clearing bush/cutting stems; B - weeding, making ridges/mounds; C - harvesting rice/cutting grass; D - levelling seedbeds/gathering trash; E - digging/turning soil, transplanting (1 mark each)
3 marks: (c) Any three: clean after use; sharpen regularly; oil/grease to prevent rust; fix loose handle; store in a dry place (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d) Any two: wear boots/gloves; cut away from the body; do not swing near others; carry with blade pointing downward; keep in a sheath (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A cutlass, B hoe, C sickle, D rake, E spade. (b) The cutlass clears bush, the hoe weeds and makes ridges, the sickle harvests grass and rice, the rake levels seedbeds and the spade digs. (c) Clean, sharpen, oil and store the cutlass dry. (d) Cut away from the body and wear protective boots.

questions.topic: Practical: Tractor and animal drawn implements
questions.stem:
Study the tractor-coupled implements described below.
Implement F: a frame carrying three or four large concave steel discs, each set at an angle to the direction of travel; it cuts and inverts the soil to a good depth.
Implement G: a frame with a large number of smaller concave discs arranged in two gangs set at opposite angles; used after F.
Implement H: a frame carrying two or more double-sided (mouldboard-like) bodies that throw soil to both sides, forming raised rows.
Implement I: a frame carrying seed hoppers, metering mechanisms and furrow openers, with press wheels behind.
(a) Identify implements F, G, H and I. [4 marks]
(b) State the function of each implement. [4 marks]
(c) State the correct order in which F, G and H are used in seedbed preparation. [2 marks]
(d) State three maintenance practices for implement F. [3 marks]
(e) State two advantages of using I over manual planting. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) F - disc plough; G - disc harrow; H - ridger; I - planter (seed drill) (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) F - primary tillage: cutting and turning the soil; G - secondary tillage: breaking clods and levelling; H - making ridges; I - sowing seeds at uniform depth and spacing (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) F (ploughing), then G (harrowing), then H (ridging)
3 marks: (d) Any three: clean after use; grease bearings/lubricate moving parts; tighten loose nuts and bolts; replace worn discs; store under shed; paint/oil to prevent rust (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e) Any two: faster/covers large area; uniform spacing and depth; saves labour; correct seed rate/less wastage (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) F disc plough, G disc harrow, H ridger, I planter. (b) The plough cuts and inverts soil, the harrow breaks clods, the ridger forms ridges and the planter sows seeds evenly. (c) Plough, then harrow, then ridge. (d) Clean, grease bearings, tighten bolts and store under shelter. (e) A planter is faster, saves labour and gives uniform spacing and depth.

questions.topic: Practical: Farm surveying equipment
questions.stem:
A group of students surveyed a farm plot using the following equipment.
Item J: a metal chain made of 100 links, 20.1 m (66 feet) long, with handles at both ends.
Item K: a long graduated flexible strip of fibreglass or steel wound in a case.
Item L: a straight pole about 2 m long painted alternately in red and white bands, with a pointed metal tip.
Item M: a hand-held instrument with a magnetic needle and a sighting prism, used to read bearings.
The students found that the plot was made up of a rectangle 60 m long and 45 m wide, and an adjoining right-angled triangle whose two shorter sides were 40 m and 30 m.
(a) Identify items J, K, L and M. [4 marks]
(b) State one use of each of items L and M. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate (i) the area of the rectangle; (ii) the area of the triangle; (iii) the total area of the plot in hectares. [6 marks]
(d) State three maintenance practices for item J or K. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) J - Gunter's chain (surveyor's chain); K - measuring tape; L - ranging pole; M - prismatic compass (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) L - marking points/stations and lining out straight lines; M - measuring bearings/direction (1 mark each)
6 marks: (c)(i) 60 x 45 = 2,700 m2 (2); (ii) 1/2 x 40 x 30 = 600 m2 (2); (iii) 2,700 + 600 = 3,300 m2 = 0.33 ha (2)
3 marks: (d) Any three: clean and dry after use; oil steel chain/tape to prevent rust; wind tape back carefully/avoid kinks; store in a dry place; repair broken links (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) J is a Gunter's chain, K a measuring tape, L a ranging pole and M a prismatic compass. (b) Ranging poles mark stations and line out straight lines; the compass measures bearings. (c) Rectangle = 60 x 45 = 2,700 m2; triangle = 0.5 x 40 x 30 = 600 m2; total = 3,300 m2 = 3,300/10,000 = 0.33 ha. (d) Clean, oil, wind carefully and store dry.

questions.topic: Practical: Planting dates, seed rates, plant population and seed quality tests
questions.stem:
A farmer in Zaria wants to plant 1 hectare of maize at a spacing of 75 cm x 25 cm with one seed per hole. A germination test was carried out on 100 seeds from the seed lot and 85 seeds germinated. A purity test on a 200 g sample showed 190 g of pure maize seed, the rest being chaff, broken seeds and weed seeds. The mass of 1,000 maize seeds is 300 g.
(a) Calculate (i) the percentage germination; (ii) the percentage purity. [2 marks]
(b) Calculate the real value (pure live seed) of the seed lot, using real value = (germination % x purity %) / 100. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the plant population per hectare (to the nearest whole plant). [3 marks]
(d) Calculate the mass of seed (in kg) needed for 1 hectare (i) assuming all seeds germinate; (ii) adjusted for the germination percentage, to two decimal places. [4 marks]
(e) Describe how the germination test was carried out. [2 marks]
(f) State two factors that determine the seed rate of a crop. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) 85/100 x 100 = 85%; (ii) 190/200 x 100 = 95% (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) 85 x 95 / 100 = 80.75%
3 marks: (c) Area per plant = 0.75 x 0.25 = 0.1875 m2 (1); 10,000 / 0.1875 = 53,333 plants (2)
4 marks: (d)(i) 53,333 x 0.3 g = 16,000 g = 16.0 kg (2); (ii) 16.0 / 0.85 = 18.82 kg (2)
2 marks: (e) Place a counted number of seeds (100) on moist cotton wool/filter paper in a Petri dish or in moist sand in a germination box, keep moist and warm, count seeds that germinate after 5-7 days
2 marks: (f) Any two: spacing/plant population; seed size/weight; germination percentage/viability; purity; method of planting; number of seeds per hole (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) Germination = 85/100 x 100 = 85%; purity = 190/200 x 100 = 95%. (b) Real value = 85 x 95/100 = 80.75%. (c) Each plant occupies 0.75 x 0.25 = 0.1875 m2; population = 10,000/0.1875 = 53,333 plants per hectare. (d) Mass per seed = 300/1,000 = 0.3 g; 53,333 x 0.3 = 15,999.9 g, about 16.0 kg; adjusting for 85% germination: 16.0/0.85 = 18.82 kg. (e) Seeds are placed on moist cotton wool or sand, kept warm and moist, and germinated seeds counted after about a week. (f) Seed rate depends on spacing, seed size and germination percentage.

questions.topic: Practical: Seeds, seedlings, fruits and storage organs of crops
questions.stem:
Study the planting materials described below.
Specimen A: a large, cylindrical, brown-skinned underground storage organ with a rough surface; when cut, the flesh is white; planting material is obtained by cutting it into setts.
Specimen B: a woody stem piece about 25 cm long with nodes and buds, taken from a plant whose roots are swollen with starch.
Specimen C: a rounded underground stem, brown and hairy, with rings (nodes) and a terminal bud; small daughter structures (cormels) are attached.
Specimen D: an underground organ made of fleshy leaf bases wrapped round a short stem, with a cluster of fibrous roots at the base.
Specimen E: a horizontal, branched, fleshy underground stem with nodes, scale leaves and a pungent smell.
(a) Identify each of specimens A to E, naming the crop and the type of organ (e.g. tuber, corm). [5 marks]
(b) State the method of propagation of each of A, B and C. [3 marks]
(c) State two ways of storing specimen A. [2 marks]
(d) State three advantages of vegetative propagation. [3 marks]
(e) State two disadvantages of vegetative propagation. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - yam (stem tuber); B - cassava (stem cutting); C - cocoyam (corm); D - onion (bulb); E - ginger (rhizome) (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b) A - setts/minisetts or whole seed yams; B - stem cuttings; C - corms/cormels (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Any two: yam barn; storing in pits/underground; cool, dry, well-ventilated store; on raised platforms (1 mark each)
3 marks: (d) Any three: offspring identical to parent (true to type); early maturity; easier where seeds are not viable; ensures survival of good varieties (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e) Any two: transmits diseases from parent; bulky planting material; no variation; overcrowding (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A yam tuber, B cassava stem cutting, C cocoyam corm, D onion bulb, E ginger rhizome. (b) Yam is propagated by setts or minisetts, cassava by stem cuttings and cocoyam by corms or cormels. (c) Yams are stored in yam barns or cool ventilated rooms. (d) Vegetative propagation gives true-to-type, early-maturing plants. (e) It spreads disease and the material is bulky.

questions.topic: Practical: Main pests and diseases of crops
questions.stem:
Study the pests described below.
Specimen F: a large, brightly coloured (yellow, black and red) grasshopper that produces a foul-smelling foam when handled; it feeds on leaves of cassava and other crops.
Specimen G: a caterpillar found boring inside the stems of maize plants, making holes and leaving frass (sawdust-like droppings); infested plants show dead hearts.
Specimen H: a small brownish beetle with a long snout, found in large numbers in stored maize grain, which develops holes and powdery dust.
Specimen I: a sap-sucking bug collected from cocoa pods with black, sunken lesions on them.
(a) Identify specimens F, G, H and I. [4 marks]
(b) State the type of mouthparts of (i) F; (ii) I. [2 marks]
(c) Describe the damage caused by each of G and H. [4 marks]
(d) State one cultural method and one chemical method of controlling G. [2 marks]
(e) State three ways of preventing the damage caused by H in storage. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) F - variegated grasshopper (Zonocerus variegatus); G - maize stem borer larva; H - maize weevil (Sitophilus zeamais); I - cocoa mirid (capsid) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Biting and chewing; (ii) piercing and sucking (1 mark each)
4 marks: (c) G - bores into stem, eats tissues, weakens stem causing lodging, dead heart and low yield (2); H - bores into grains, eats contents, reducing weight, quality and viability of grain (2)
2 marks: (d) Cultural: early planting/crop rotation/destroying crop residues; chemical: application of systemic insecticide (e.g. granules in leaf funnel) (1 mark each)
3 marks: (e) Any three: dry grains properly before storage; clean and fumigate store; use hermetic (airtight) bags/containers; treat with approved storage insecticide; store on pallets/in cribs (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) F is the variegated grasshopper, G the maize stem borer, H the maize weevil and I the cocoa mirid (capsid). (b) Grasshoppers have biting and chewing mouthparts; mirids have piercing and sucking mouthparts. (c) Stem borers tunnel in stems, causing dead heart and lodging; weevils bore into grains, reducing weight and viability. (d) Stem borers are controlled by early planting and burning residues, or by systemic insecticides. (e) Dry grain well, fumigate stores and use hermetic bags.

questions.topic: Practical: Common weeds
questions.stem:
Study the weeds described below.
Specimen A: a perennial grass with sharp-pointed, white underground rhizomes and long narrow leaves with a prominent white midrib; it regrows quickly after burning.
Specimen B: a low, spreading herb of the daisy family with hairy stems, leaves in opposite pairs with toothed margins, and small yellow-and-white flower heads on long stalks.
Specimen C: an annual herb with hairy stems, opposite oval leaves and small bluish-purple flowers in clusters, with a goat-like smell.
Specimen D: a small plant with bright pink-red flowers found attached to the roots of sorghum and maize plants, which are stunted and yellow.
Specimen E: a floating aquatic plant with swollen spongy leaf stalks, glossy green leaves and pale violet flowers, forming dense mats on rivers.
(a) Identify specimens A to E. [5 marks]
(b) State two features that make A difficult to control. [2 marks]
(c) Explain how D harms its host crops. [2 marks]
(d) State two problems caused by E. [2 marks]
(e) State two cultural and two chemical methods of weed control. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - spear grass (Imperata cylindrica); B - Tridax procumbens (coat buttons); C - goat weed (Ageratum conyzoides); D - witchweed (Striga); E - water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b) Any two: deep, extensive rhizomes regenerate after slashing/burning; sharp rhizome tips pierce tubers/roots; produces many wind-dispersed seeds (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) It is a parasite that attaches to the roots of the host and draws water, mineral salts and food from it, causing stunting, yellowing and yield loss
2 marks: (d) Any two: blocks waterways/navigation; clogs irrigation channels and fishing nets; reduces oxygen in water killing fish; breeding site for mosquitoes/snails (1 mark each)
4 marks: (e) Cultural (any two): hand weeding/hoeing; mulching; crop rotation; cover cropping; close spacing; Chemical (any two): pre-emergence herbicide e.g. atrazine; post-emergence herbicide e.g. glyphosate/paraquat; selective herbicide e.g. 2,4-D (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A spear grass, B Tridax, C goat weed (Ageratum), D Striga (witchweed), E water hyacinth. (b) Spear grass regrows from deep rhizomes and its sharp rhizomes pierce crop roots. (c) Striga parasitises cereal roots, drawing water and nutrients so the host is stunted. (d) Water hyacinth blocks waterways and irrigation channels and depletes oxygen. (e) Cultural: hand weeding, mulching; chemical: glyphosate, atrazine.

questions.topic: Practical: Common breeds and types of animals
questions.stem:
Study the farm animals described below.
Animal A: a large, white humped cow with long lyre-shaped horns, a large dewlap and long legs; commonly herded in northern Nigeria.
Animal B: a small, humpless, short-horned cow, black or black-and-white, resistant to trypanosomiasis; found in southern Nigeria.
Animal C: a fawn or black humpless cow with medium horns, also trypanotolerant, originally from Guinea.
Animal D: a large white pig with erect ears and a long body.
Animal E: a small goat, about 50 cm tall, with short legs, found in the humid forest zone; very prolific.
(a) Identify each animal by breed name. [5 marks]
(b) State which of A, B and C are (i) zebu (Bos indicus) types; (ii) humpless (Bos taurus) types. [2 marks]
(c) State two characteristics that make B and C suitable for southern Nigeria. [2 marks]
(d) State the main purpose for which each of D and E is reared. [2 marks]
(e) State four reasons why exotic breeds are crossed with local breeds. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - White Fulani (Bunaji); B - Muturu; C - N'Dama; D - Large White; E - West African Dwarf goat (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) A; (ii) B and C (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Any two: tolerant/resistant to trypanosomiasis; small size suited to forest zone; tolerant of heat and humidity; hardy on poor forage (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d) D - meat (pork/bacon); E - meat (chevon) and skin (1 mark each)
4 marks: (e) Any four: improve growth rate; increase milk/meat yield; combine disease resistance and adaptation of local with high productivity of exotic; hybrid vigour; improve feed conversion (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A White Fulani, B Muturu, C N'Dama, D Large White pig, E West African Dwarf goat. (b) White Fulani is a zebu; Muturu and N'Dama are humpless. (c) Muturu and N'Dama tolerate trypanosomiasis and humid heat. (d) Large White is kept for pork, the dwarf goat for meat and skin. (e) Crossing combines local hardiness with exotic productivity and gives hybrid vigour.

questions.topic: Practical: Major internal organs of farm animals
questions.stem:
The following organs were removed from farm animals and are described below.
Organ A: a thin-walled bag at the base of the neck of a fowl, which contained whole maize grains.
Organ B: a hard, thick-walled muscular organ from a fowl, with a tough inner lining, containing small stones (grit).
Organ C: the largest of four stomach compartments of a cow, containing fermenting grass.
Organ D: a stomach compartment of a cow with a honeycomb-like inner lining.
Organ E: a stomach compartment of a cow with many leaf-like folds.
(a) Identify organs A to E. [5 marks]
(b) State the function of each of A and B. [4 marks]
(c) Name the fourth stomach compartment of the cow and state its function. [2 marks]
(d) Explain why the cow is described as a ruminant. [2 marks]
(e) Why does a fowl swallow grit? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - crop; B - gizzard; C - rumen; D - reticulum; E - omasum (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) A - stores and softens food (2); B - grinds food with the aid of grit (2)
2 marks: (c) Abomasum (true stomach) (1); secretes gastric juice for enzymatic digestion (1)
2 marks: (d) It chews the cud - regurgitates partly digested food from the rumen and chews it again
2 marks: (e) The grit in the gizzard helps to grind food because birds have no teeth
questions.explanation: (a) A crop, B gizzard, C rumen, D reticulum, E omasum. (b) The crop stores and softens food; the gizzard grinds it with grit. (c) The abomasum is the true stomach that secretes digestive enzymes. (d) A ruminant chews the cud, regurgitating food from the rumen for further chewing. (e) Birds have no teeth, so grit helps grind food.

questions.topic: Practical: Animal feeds and feed stuffs
questions.stem:
A poultry farmer in Ogun State wants to compound 500 kg of a grower ration containing 16% crude protein, using only maize (9% crude protein) and soybean meal (44% crude protein).
(a) Using the Pearson square method, calculate (i) the parts of maize and soybean meal required; (ii) the percentage of each in the ration. [5 marks]
(b) Calculate the mass of each feedstuff needed for 500 kg of ration. [2 marks]
(c) Show that the ration contains 16% crude protein. [2 marks]
(d) Classify maize and soybean meal as energy or protein concentrates. [2 marks]
(e) State two other ingredients that must be added to make a complete ration and the purpose of each. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a)(i) Maize: 44 - 16 = 28 parts; soybean meal: 16 - 9 = 7 parts; total 35 parts (3); (ii) maize 28/35 x 100 = 80%; soybean meal 7/35 x 100 = 20% (2)
2 marks: (b) Maize 0.80 x 500 = 400 kg; soybean meal 0.20 x 500 = 100 kg (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) (400 x 9% + 100 x 44%) = 36 + 44 = 80 kg protein; 80/500 x 100 = 16%
2 marks: (d) Maize - energy concentrate; soybean meal - protein concentrate (1 mark each)
4 marks: (e) Any two x 2 marks: bone meal/oyster shell - calcium and phosphorus for bones/eggshell; salt - sodium and chlorine/palatability; vitamin-mineral premix - vitamins and trace elements; lysine/methionine - essential amino acids
questions.explanation: (a) Pearson square: place 16 in the centre, maize 9 and soybean meal 44 on the left; differences give maize 44 - 16 = 28 parts and soybean 16 - 9 = 7 parts; total 35. Maize = 28/35 = 80%, soybean meal = 7/35 = 20%. (b) Maize 400 kg, soybean meal 100 kg. (c) Protein = 400 x 0.09 + 100 x 0.44 = 36 + 44 = 80 kg; 80/500 x 100 = 16%. (d) Maize is an energy concentrate; soybean meal a protein concentrate. (e) Bone meal or oyster shell supply calcium and phosphorus; vitamin-mineral premix supplies vitamins and trace elements; salt adds sodium.

questions.topic: Practical: Main pests and parasites of farm animals
questions.stem:
Study the parasites described below.
Specimen A: an oval, flattened, eight-legged arthropod, swollen with blood, found attached to the ears and udder of cattle.
Specimen B: a brown fly, with wings folded over each other like closed scissors when at rest, and a long piercing proboscis.
Specimen C: a long, flat, white, ribbon-like worm made up of many segments, found in the small intestine of a pig.
Specimen D: a flat, leaf-shaped worm found in the bile ducts of a sheep.
Specimen E: tiny wingless insects found among the feathers of fowls.
(a) Identify specimens A to E. [5 marks]
(b) Classify each of A, C and D as ectoparasite or endoparasite. [3 marks]
(c) Name one disease transmitted by each of A and B. [2 marks]
(d) Name the intermediate host of D. [1 mark]
(e) State four general effects of parasites on farm animals. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - tick; B - tsetse fly; C - tapeworm; D - liver fluke; E - lice (poultry lice) (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b) A - ectoparasite; C - endoparasite; D - endoparasite (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) A - heartwater/redwater (babesiosis)/anaplasmosis; B - trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness/nagana) (1 mark each)
1 mark: (d) Water snail (Lymnaea)
4 marks: (e) Any four: suck blood causing anaemia; loss of weight/poor growth; transmit diseases; damage hides/skin and organs; reduce production (milk, eggs, meat); death in severe cases (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A tick, B tsetse fly, C tapeworm, D liver fluke, E lice. (b) The tick is an ectoparasite; tapeworm and liver fluke are endoparasites. (c) Ticks transmit heartwater and babesiosis; tsetse flies transmit trypanosomiasis. (d) The liver fluke's intermediate host is the water snail Lymnaea. (e) Parasites cause anaemia, weight loss, damaged hides, reduced output and disease.

questions.topic: Practical: Diseases of farm animals
questions.stem:
The symptoms observed in four sick animals on a farm are described below.
Case A: in a flock of broilers, birds gasp for breath, have greenish diarrhoea, twisted necks and paralysis; many die suddenly.
Case B: in a flock of young chicks, birds have bloody droppings, ruffled feathers and drooping wings; the litter is wet.
Case C: in a herd of cattle, animals have blisters on the mouth, tongue and between the hooves, drool saliva and limp.
Case D: in cattle grazing near a wooded river bank, animals are weak, anaemic and emaciated with intermittent fever.
(a) Name the disease in each of cases A, B, C and D. [4 marks]
(b) Name the causative organism (type) of each disease. [4 marks]
(c) State one preventive measure for each of A and B. [2 marks]
(d) State two general measures for controlling disease outbreaks on a farm. [2 marks]
(e) State three signs of good health in farm animals. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) A - Newcastle disease; B - coccidiosis; C - foot-and-mouth disease; D - trypanosomiasis (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) A - virus; B - protozoa (Eimeria); C - virus; D - protozoa (Trypanosoma) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) A - vaccination (e.g. Lasota/Komarov); B - keep litter dry/use coccidiostats in feed or water (1 mark each)
2 marks: (d) Any two: isolate sick animals; quarantine new stock; proper disposal of dead animals; disinfection of pens/foot dips; vaccination; restrict visitors (1 mark each)
3 marks: (e) Any three: alert and active; good appetite; bright eyes; smooth/shiny coat or feathers; normal droppings; normal temperature and breathing (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A Newcastle disease, B coccidiosis, C foot-and-mouth disease, D trypanosomiasis. (b) Newcastle and foot-and-mouth are viral; coccidiosis (Eimeria) and trypanosomiasis (Trypanosoma) are protozoan. (c) Vaccinate against Newcastle; keep litter dry and use coccidiostats. (d) Isolate sick animals and disinfect pens. (e) Healthy animals are alert, eat well and have bright eyes and shiny coats.

questions.topic: Practical: Routine management practices in farm animals
questions.stem:
Study the tools and practices described below.
Tool A: a heavy pincer-like instrument with blunt jaws used to crush the spermatic cords of a bull calf without cutting the skin.
Tool B: a device with a heated blade used to cut and cauterise the tip of the upper beak of pullets.
Tool C: a pair of pliers that cuts V-shaped pieces from the edge of the ears of piglets.
Tool D: a hot iron or caustic stick applied to the horn buds of young calves.
(a) Identify tools A to D. [4 marks]
(b) Name the management practice carried out with each tool. [4 marks]
(c) State one reason for each practice in (b). [4 marks]
(d) State three other routine management practices in pig production. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) A - burdizzo (emasculator); B - debeaker; C - ear notcher; D - dehorning iron/caustic stick (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b) A - castration; B - debeaking; C - ear notching (identification); D - disbudding/dehorning (1 mark each)
4 marks: (c) Castration - docile animals, better meat quality/prevents unwanted breeding; debeaking - prevents feather pecking and cannibalism; ear notching - identification/record keeping; dehorning - prevents injury to animals and handlers (1 mark each)
3 marks: (d) Any three: teeth clipping (needle teeth); iron injection; tail docking; deworming; weaning; vaccination; castration of boars (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A burdizzo, B debeaker, C ear notcher, D dehorning iron. (b) They are used for castration, debeaking, ear notching and dehorning. (c) Castration makes animals docile and prevents unwanted mating; debeaking prevents cannibalism; ear notching identifies animals; dehorning prevents injury. (d) In pigs: clipping needle teeth, iron injection and tail docking.

questions.topic: Practical: Livestock and fishing equipment
questions.stem:
A poultry farmer keeps 500 laying birds in a deep litter house. The equipment includes items described below.
Item A: a round plastic container with an inverted jar that releases water into a shallow trough as the birds drink.
Item B: a long metal trough with a rotating bar (reel) on top.
Item C: a canopy-covered heat source used for day-old chicks.
Item D: a wooden box partitioned into compartments, lined with straw, where hens lay.
The number of eggs collected over one week were: Monday 410, Tuesday 420, Wednesday 405, Thursday 415, Friday 425, Saturday 400, Sunday 430. Each bird eats 120 g of feed per day.
(a) Identify items A to D and state the function of B's rotating bar. [5 marks]
(b) Calculate (i) the total number of eggs laid in the week; (ii) the average daily egg production; (iii) the hen-day egg production percentage. [5 marks]
(c) How many full crates of 30 eggs were collected, and how many eggs were left over? [2 marks]
(d) Calculate the total quantity of feed (in kg) consumed in the week. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
5 marks: (a) A - drinker (fount); B - feeder (feeding trough); C - brooder; D - laying nest (1 mark each); rotating bar prevents birds from perching on and fouling/wasting feed (1)
5 marks: (b)(i) 2,905 eggs (2); (ii) 2,905/7 = 415 eggs per day (1); (iii) 415/500 x 100 = 83% (2)
2 marks: (c) 2,905/30 = 96 full crates (1), 25 eggs left over (1)
3 marks: (d) 500 x 120 g x 7 = 420,000 g (2) = 420 kg (1)
questions.explanation: (a) A drinker, B feeder, C brooder, D laying nest; the reel on the feeder stops birds perching and fouling or scratching out feed. (b) Total = 410+420+405+415+425+400+430 = 2,905 eggs; average = 2,905/7 = 415 eggs/day; hen-day production = 415/500 x 100 = 83%. (c) 2,905 = 96 x 30 + 25, so 96 crates with 25 eggs left. (d) Feed = 500 x 0.12 kg x 7 = 420 kg.

questions.topic: Farm records and accounts
questions.stem:
A farmer near Minna cultivated 2 hectares of maize in the 2025 season. The records were:
Ploughing and harrowing by hired tractor: 2 ha at ₦70,000 per ha
Seed: 50 kg at ₦2,500 per kg
Fertiliser: 12 bags at ₦45,000 per bag
Herbicide: 10 litres at ₦8,000 per litre
Hired labour (planting, weeding, harvesting): ₦300,000
Transport of produce: ₦100,000
Knapsack sprayer bought for ₦60,000, expected to last 4 years with no scrap value.
Yield: 2.5 tonnes per hectare, sold at ₦500,000 per tonne.
(a) Calculate the total variable cost. [4 marks]
(b) Calculate the total revenue. [2 marks]
(c) Calculate the gross margin. [2 marks]
(d) Calculate the annual depreciation of the sprayer by the straight-line method. [2 marks]
(e) Calculate the net profit. [2 marks]
(f) Calculate the cost of producing one tonne of maize (total cost / output). [3 marks]

questions.topic: Practical: Methods of propagation of horticultural plants
questions.stem:
Four methods of propagating horticultural plants were demonstrated on a school farm.
Method A: a bud with a small piece of bark was cut from a sweet orange tree and inserted into a T-shaped cut on the stem of a rough lemon seedling, then tied with polythene tape.
Method B: a shoot of a mango variety was cut obliquely and joined to a similarly cut stem of a mango seedling of equal thickness, and the union tied firmly.
Method C: a ring of bark was removed from a branch of a hibiscus plant still attached to the parent, moist soil wrapped round the wound and covered with polythene until roots formed.
Method D: pieces of Ixora stem with three nodes were inserted into a box of moist sand under shade.
(a) Name each of methods A to D. [4 marks]
(b) In method A, name (i) the sweet orange part; (ii) the rough lemon seedling. [2 marks]
(c) State two reasons for tying the union with polythene tape in A. [2 marks]
(d) State three conditions necessary for the success of method B. [3 marks]
(e) State four advantages of propagating fruit trees by methods A and B. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) A - budding (T-budding); B - grafting (splice/whip grafting); C - marcotting (air layering); D - stem cuttings (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Scion (bud); (ii) rootstock (stock) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (c) Any two: hold bud firmly in contact with stock; prevent drying out; prevent entry of water and pathogens (1 mark each)
3 marks: (d) Any three: stock and scion compatible (same/closely related species); cambium layers in close contact; clean sharp knife; carried out when plants are actively growing; union protected from drying (1 mark each)
4 marks: (e) Any four: early fruiting; true-to-type fruit; combines good fruit with hardy/disease-resistant rootstock; shorter trees easier to harvest; can repair damaged trees/change variety (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A budding, B grafting, C marcotting (air layering), D stem cuttings. (b) The sweet orange bud is the scion; the rough lemon is the rootstock. (c) Tying holds the bud in place and prevents drying and infection. (d) Stock and scion must be compatible, cambia matched, and a clean sharp knife used. (e) Budded and grafted trees fruit early, are true to type and combine good fruit with hardy rootstocks.

questions.topic: Practical: Irrigation and drainage
questions.stem:
Study the equipment described below.
Item A: a can with a long spout ending in a perforated rose.
Item B: a rotating nozzle on a riser pipe connected to a pump, throwing water in a circle like rain.
Item C: thin plastic pipes laid along crop rows, with small emitters that release water drop by drop near each plant.
Item D: perforated clay or plastic pipes laid in trenches below the soil surface and covered with gravel, leading to an open ditch.
A farmer in Kano wants to apply 25 mm of water to a vegetable bed 20 m long and 10 m wide.
(a) Identify items A to D. [4 marks]
(b) Which of the items is used for drainage? [1 mark]
(c) Calculate the volume of water needed for the bed (i) in cubic metres; (ii) in litres. [4 marks]
(d) How many full cans of A (capacity 10 litres) are needed? [2 marks]
(e) If 400 plants on drip irrigation each receive 2 litres per day, calculate the daily water use. [2 marks]
(f) State two advantages of C over B. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a) A - watering can; B - sprinkler; C - drip (trickle) irrigation line; D - subsurface (tile) drain (1 mark each)
1 mark: (b) D
4 marks: (c)(i) 20 x 10 x 0.025 = 5 m3 (2); (ii) 5 x 1,000 = 5,000 litres (2)
2 marks: (d) 5,000 / 10 = 500 cans
2 marks: (e) 400 x 2 = 800 litres per day
2 marks: (f) Any two: saves water; less evaporation loss; water applied directly to roots; fewer weeds between rows; can apply fertiliser with water; no leaf wetting/fewer leaf diseases (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A watering can, B sprinkler, C drip line, D subsurface drain. (b) D is used for drainage. (c) Volume = 20 x 10 x 0.025 m = 5 m3 = 5,000 litres. (d) 5,000/10 = 500 cans. (e) 400 x 2 = 800 litres per day. (f) Drip irrigation saves water, reduces evaporation and weeds and keeps leaves dry.

questions.topic: Practical: Fish harvesting and preservation
questions.stem:
Study the items described below.
Item A: a long, rectangular net with floats on top and weights at the bottom, set across a river so that fish are trapped by their gills.
Item B: a circular net with weights round its edge, thrown by hand to spread over the water and sink over fish.
Item C: a drum-like or brick structure with wire mesh trays above a fire, used to dry fish with smoke and heat.
A fish farmer harvested 50 kg of fresh catfish. After gutting (removing the internal organs) the fish weighed 44 kg. After smoking in item C, the smoked fish weighed 15 kg.
(a) Identify items A, B and C. [3 marks]
(b) Calculate (i) the dressing percentage (gutted mass as % of fresh mass); (ii) smoked mass as a percentage of fresh mass; (iii) smoked mass as a percentage of gutted mass, to one decimal place. [6 marks]
(c) Explain why the fish lost mass during smoking. [2 marks]
(d) State two other methods of fish preservation. [2 marks]
(e) State two precautions to observe when using item A. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a) A - gill net; B - cast net; C - smoking kiln (smoker) (1 mark each)
6 marks: (b)(i) 44/50 x 100 = 88% (2); (ii) 15/50 x 100 = 30% (2); (iii) 15/44 x 100 = 34.1% (2)
2 marks: (c) Heat evaporated water from the fish tissues (moisture loss)
2 marks: (d) Any two: freezing/refrigeration; salting; sun drying; canning; frying (1 mark each)
2 marks: (e) Any two: use the approved mesh size to avoid catching juvenile fish; check nets regularly to remove catch before it spoils; mend torn nets; dry and store nets after use (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) A gill net, B cast net, C smoking kiln. (b) Dressing percentage = 44/50 x 100 = 88%; smoked/fresh = 15/50 x 100 = 30%; smoked/gutted = 15/44 x 100 = 34.1%. (c) Heat and smoke drove water out of the flesh. (d) Freezing, salting and sun drying also preserve fish. (e) Use legal mesh sizes and check and mend nets regularly.
